author: A Robot
objectives: Students will identify and name the four chambers of the heart, the four heart valves, and the major vessels entering and leaving the heart.
Students will trace the path of blood through the heart's dual circulation, naming each chamber, valve, and vessel in order.
Students will distinguish the pulmonary circuit from the systemic circuit and explain why the right and left sides of the heart serve different circulatory functions.

Students will explain why the left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium than the right ventricle, relating wall thickness to the pressure required to perfuse the systemic versus pulmonary circuits.
Students will describe the function of the atrioventricular and semilunar valves in preventing backflow, and identify which valves separate which chambers or chamber-vessel pairs.

modules.moduleName: Heart Anatomy: Chambers and Major Vessels
modules.description: A guided exploration of the external anatomy of the human heart, introducing students to the four chambers, the major vessels entering and leaving the heart, and the relationship between chamber position and function.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the four chambers of the heart and their locations on the anatomical heart model.
Recognize and locate the superior vena cava, inferior vena cava, pulmonary arteries, pulmonary veins, and aorta on the heart.
Understand the relationship between vessel entry/exit points and the dual-loop circulation.
Visualize the difference in wall thickness between the left and right ventricles.

clips.changeMeaning: The complete heart model is rendered and positioned in the workspace. Text labels for the four chambers appear with the main heart object.
clips.narration: Welcome to the cardiac anatomy lab. Today we're exploring the structure of the human heart, one of the most vital organs in the body. You'll see a model of the heart positioned in front of you. The heart is divided into four chambers: two upper chambers called atria and two lower chambers called ventricles.

clips.changeMeaning: Chamber labels become visible, highlighting each chamber's position and role in circulation. The heart is highlighted with chamber-specific colors to emphasize anatomy.
clips.narration: The right atrium sits on the right side of the heart and receives deoxygenated blood returning from the body. Below it is the right ventricle, which pumps that blood to the lungs. On the left side, the left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood returning from the lungs. Below it, the left ventricle pumps blood out to the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: Major vessels appear around the heart model. Each vessel is colored to indicate whether it carries oxygenated blood (bright red) or deoxygenated blood (dark blue), and positioned to show entry and exit points.
clips.narration: Now let's look at the major blood vessels connected to the heart. The superior and inferior vena cava deliver deoxygenated blood from the body into the right atrium. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. The pulmonary veins return oxygen-rich blood from the lungs to the left atrium. Finally, the aorta is the largest artery, exiting the left ventricle to supply the entire body.

clips.changeMeaning: The heart model is updated to emphasize the difference in wall thickness. The left ventricle is visually thickened to show its muscular mass relative to the right ventricle.
clips.narration: Notice the difference in wall thickness between the left and right ventricles. The left ventricle has a substantially thicker myocardium—the muscular wall—than the right ventricle. Because the left ventricle must generate much higher pressure to pump blood throughout the entire body. The right ventricle only needs to pump blood a short distance to the nearby lungs. This difference in wall thickness reflects the different workloads of each ventricle.

modules.description: A step-by-step animation tracing the complete path of blood through the heart, highlighting chambers, valves, and vessels in sequence. Students follow the dual-loop circulation from the systemic return through the pulmonary circuit and back to systemic distribution.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Trace the complete path of deoxygenated blood entering the right atrium and exiting via the pulmonary arteries.
Trace the complete path of oxygenated blood entering the left atrium and exiting via the aorta.
Identify the four heart valves and their roles in preventing backflow.
Explain the sequential nature of the cardiac cycle: atrial filling, atrial contraction, ventricular filling, and ventricular contraction.

clips.changeMeaning: A blue blood droplet appears approaching the right atrium from above, indicating deoxygenated blood returning from systemic circulation. A label explains systemic return.
clips.narration: Let's trace the journey of blood through the heart, starting with deoxygenated blood returning from the body. Blood that has delivered its oxygen to the body tissues is collected by the superior and inferior vena cava. This deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium, filling it during diastole—the relaxation phase of the cardiac cycle.

clips.changeMeaning: The blood droplet moves from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The tricuspid valve label appears, highlighting its location and function.
clips.narration: When the right atrium contracts, it pushes blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. The tricuspid valve is an atrioventricular valve—it sits between an atrium and a ventricle and prevents backflow when the ventricle contracts. Notice it has three leaflets, hence the name 'tricuspid.'

clips.changeMeaning: The blood droplet exits the right ventricle through the pulmonary valve and travels upward toward the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary valve label appears.
clips.narration: Now the right ventricle contracts, pumping deoxygenated blood upward through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary arteries. The pulmonary valve is a semilunar valve, with three half-moon-shaped leaflets that prevent blood from flowing backward into the ventricle. The pulmonary arteries carry this blood to both lungs, where gas exchange occurs.

clips.changeMeaning: The blood droplet color changes from dark blue to bright red, and it moves from the pulmonary area to the left atrium. A label indicates oxygenated blood returning from lungs.
clips.narration: After gas exchange in the lungs, the now oxygen-rich blood is collected by the pulmonary veins and returns to the left side of the heart. The pulmonary veins deliver this oxygenated blood directly into the left atrium.

clips.changeMeaning: The red blood droplet moves from the left atrium through the mitral valve into the left ventricle. The mitral valve label appears, noting its two leaflets.
clips.narration: When the left atrium contracts, it pushes blood through the mitral valve—also called the bicuspid valve because it has two leaflets—into the left ventricle. The mitral valve is the second atrioventricular valve, located on the left side of the heart.

clips.changeMeaning: The red blood droplet exits the left ventricle through the aortic valve and travels upward into the aorta. The aortic valve label appears. The cycle is now complete, ready to repeat.
clips.narration: Finally, the left ventricle contracts powerfully, pushing oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. The aortic valve is the second semilunar valve, and it prevents backflow into the left ventricle when the ventricle relaxes. The aorta then distributes this oxygen-rich blood throughout the entire body, completing one full cycle of circulation.

modules.description: A comparative exploration of the two circulation loops: the pulmonary circuit (right heart to lungs) and the systemic circuit (left heart to body). Students understand why the two sides of the heart are functionally different and how wall thickness relates to pressure requirements.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Distinguish between the pulmonary and systemic circuits in terms of destination, pressure, and function.
Explain why the left ventricle has thicker myocardium than the right ventricle using pressure and distance arguments.
Connect the structure of each side of the heart to the circulatory demands it must meet.
Understand the role of the lungs as a low-pressure circuit compared to the systemic circulation.

components.text: Left Ventricle: Thicker Myocardium for Body Perfusion

clips.changeMeaning: The heart is displayed centrally. The lungs model appears on the left side and body tissue on the right side, showing the two destinations for circulation.
clips.narration: The human heart drives two separate but linked circulation loops. The right side of the heart pumps blood through the pulmonary circuit—to the lungs and back—while the left side pumps blood through the systemic circuit—to all the body tissues and back. These two loops work simultaneously, with the right and left ventricles pumping in sync.

clips.changeMeaning: The lungs model is highlighted with a glow effect. A label appears identifying the pulmonary circuit and noting its low-pressure nature. The right ventricle area is emphasized with a subtle color highlight.
clips.narration: The pulmonary circuit is a short loop. The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood just to the nearby lungs—a relatively short distance requiring relatively low pressure. The lungs are designed for gas exchange, not muscular work, so they operate at low pressure. Blood quickly returns to the left atrium and is ready to be redistributed.

clips.changeMeaning: The body tissue model is highlighted. A label appears identifying the systemic circuit and noting its high-pressure nature. The left ventricle area is emphasized with a bright highlight.
clips.narration: The systemic circuit is much longer and more demanding. The left ventricle must pump blood through the aorta to every tissue in the entire body—from the brain down to the toes—and then back to the heart. This requires much higher pressure and much more muscular force than the pulmonary circuit.

clips.changeMeaning: The heart model is updated to exaggerate and highlight the difference in wall thickness between ventricles. A label appears comparing the wall thickness of the left and right ventricles, explaining the physiological basis for the difference. Both the lungs and body tissue remain visible to reinforce the connection between circuit distance/pressure and wall thickness.
clips.narration: This difference in circuit demands is reflected in the anatomy of the ventricles. The left ventricle has a much thicker myocardium than the right ventricle. The thick muscular wall of the left ventricle allows it to generate the high pressure needed to push blood throughout the systemic circulation. The thinner right ventricle is perfectly adequate for the lower-pressure pulmonary loop. Form follows function: the structure of each ventricle matches the work it must perform.
